title: Nutrition: Vitamins, Minerals, Macronutrients

sources.name: Original educational wording from general nutrition knowledge
NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: multivitamin overview (selected checks)

description: For beginners learning nutrition: macronutrients, vitamins, minerals, food sources, and basic nutrient functions. General education rather than individualized diet advice; verify with current guidelines.

cards.front: What are the three main energy-providing macronutrients?
cards.back: Carbohydrate, fat, and protein.

cards.front: About how much energy does digestible carbohydrate provide per gram?
cards.back: About 4 kilocalories per gram.

cards.front: About how much energy does protein provide per gram?
cards.back: About 4 kilocalories per gram.

cards.front: About how much energy does dietary fat provide per gram?
cards.back: About 9 kilocalories per gram.

cards.front: What does a food Calorie usually represent?
cards.back: One kilocalorie, the amount of energy commonly used on food labels.

cards.front: What is a major role of carbohydrates in the body?
cards.back: They provide glucose and other fuel for energy metabolism.

cards.front: What are monosaccharides?
cards.back: Single sugar units, such as glucose, fructose, and galactose.

cards.front: Which two sugars make up sucrose?
cards.back: Glucose and fructose.

cards.front: Which two sugars make up lactose?
cards.back: Glucose and galactose.

cards.front: What is starch?
cards.back: A digestible plant carbohydrate made of linked glucose units.

cards.front: What is glycogen?
cards.back: The storage form of glucose in animals, found especially in liver and skeletal muscle.

cards.front: How do liver and muscle glycogen serve different roles?
cards.back: Liver glycogen helps maintain blood glucose; muscle glycogen mainly fuels the muscle that stores it.

cards.front: What is dietary fiber?
cards.back: Carbohydrate material that resists digestion by human enzymes in the small intestine, with definitions also encompassing certain related substances.

cards.front: How can some soluble fibers affect digestion?
cards.back: Viscous soluble fibers can slow nutrient absorption; some help lower LDL cholesterol.

cards.front: What is a common benefit of insoluble fiber?
cards.back: It can add stool bulk and support regular bowel movements.

cards.front: What are examples of fiber-rich foods?
cards.back: Beans, lentils, whole grains, vegetables, fruits, nuts, and seeds.

cards.front: What are the three main parts of a whole grain?
cards.back: Bran, germ, and endosperm.

cards.front: How does refining grain usually change its composition?
cards.back: It removes much of the bran and germ, reducing fiber and several nutrients unless some are added back.

cards.front: What does enrichment of grain products mean?
cards.back: Adding back specified nutrients lost during processing; it does not necessarily restore fiber or every lost component.

cards.front: What is food fortification?
cards.back: Adding nutrients to a food, often to improve nutrient intake in a population.

cards.front: What are proteins made of?
cards.back: Chains of amino acids.

cards.front: What are essential amino acids?
cards.back: Amino acids the body cannot make in sufficient amounts and must obtain from food.

cards.front: How many amino acids are considered essential for healthy adults?
cards.back: Nine.

cards.front: What does protein do besides providing energy?
cards.back: It supplies material for tissues, enzymes, transport proteins, antibodies, and many signaling molecules.

cards.front: What is protein denaturation?
cards.back: A change in a protein's folded structure, such as from heat or acid, without necessarily breaking its peptide backbone.

cards.front: What does a complete dietary protein supply?
cards.back: All essential amino acids in adequate proportions relative to human needs.

cards.front: How can varied plant foods help meet amino acid needs?
cards.back: Different foods provide different amino acid patterns; a varied diet across the day can supply all essential amino acids.

cards.front: Must complementary plant proteins be eaten in the same meal by healthy adults?
cards.back: No. Overall dietary variety and adequate intake over the day are generally sufficient.

cards.front: What are triglycerides made of?
cards.back: A glycerol backbone attached to three fatty acids.

cards.front: What distinguishes saturated fatty acids structurally?
cards.back: They have no carbon-carbon double bonds in their fatty acid chains.

cards.front: What distinguishes monounsaturated fatty acids structurally?
cards.back: They have one carbon-carbon double bond.

cards.front: What distinguishes polyunsaturated fatty acids structurally?
cards.back: They have more than one carbon-carbon double bond.

cards.front: Which two fatty acids are essential in human nutrition?
cards.back: Linoleic acid, an omega-6 fatty acid, and alpha-linolenic acid, an omega-3 fatty acid.

cards.front: What does omega-3 describe in a fatty acid?
cards.back: The first double bond is at the third carbon from the methyl end.

cards.front: Which foods provide alpha-linolenic acid?
cards.back: Flaxseed, chia seeds, walnuts, and some plant oils.

cards.front: Which foods commonly provide EPA and DHA?
cards.back: Fatty fish and other seafood; some algae-derived foods or oils also provide them.

cards.front: What is one function of dietary fat in vitamin absorption?
cards.back: It supports absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.

cards.front: Does cholesterol occur naturally in ordinary plant foods?
cards.back: Plant foods generally do not supply cholesterol; they contain other sterols, such as phytosterols.

cards.front: Why is cholesterol biologically useful?
cards.back: It is a component of cell membranes and a precursor of bile acids, steroid hormones, and vitamin D.

cards.front: What is the main role of bile in fat digestion?
cards.back: Bile salts help disperse fats and form micelles, aiding digestion and absorption.

cards.front: Which vitamins are fat-soluble?
cards.back: Vitamins A, D, E, and K.

cards.front: Which vitamins are water-soluble?
cards.back: The B vitamins and vitamin C.

cards.front: Does water solubility make high-dose vitamin supplements automatically harmless?
cards.back: No. Some water-soluble vitamins can cause harm at excessive intakes.

cards.front: What are key functions of vitamin A?
cards.back: Supporting vision, epithelial tissues, and immune function.

cards.front: Which foods can provide vitamin A or its precursors?
cards.back: Liver and some dairy foods provide preformed vitamin A; orange and dark green produce can provide provitamin A carotenoids.

cards.front: Which visual problem is classically associated with vitamin A deficiency?
cards.back: Night blindness.

cards.front: What is a major function of vitamin D?
cards.back: It supports calcium and phosphate balance and normal bone mineralization.

cards.front: How can the skin contribute to vitamin D supply?
cards.back: Ultraviolet B exposure can initiate vitamin D synthesis in skin; production varies with many factors.

cards.front: What bone disorders can severe vitamin D deficiency cause?
cards.back: Rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

cards.front: Which foods can provide vitamin D?
cards.back: Fatty fish, some fortified foods, and mushrooms exposed to ultraviolet light.

cards.front: What is a major function of vitamin E?
cards.back: It acts as an antioxidant that helps protect cell membranes from oxidative damage.

cards.front: Which foods commonly provide vitamin E?
cards.back: Nuts, seeds, and vegetable oils.

cards.front: What is a major function of vitamin K?
cards.back: It is needed to activate several proteins involved in normal blood clotting and bone metabolism.

cards.front: Which foods commonly provide vitamin K1?
cards.back: Leafy green vegetables such as kale, spinach, and collard greens.

cards.front: What is vitamin B1 also called?
cards.back: Thiamin, also spelled thiamine.

cards.front: What is a major role of thiamin?
cards.back: It acts in coenzymes needed for carbohydrate metabolism and normal nerve function.

cards.front: What is vitamin B2 also called, and what does it help form?
cards.back: Riboflavin; it helps form the coenzymes FAD and FMN used in energy metabolism.

cards.front: What is vitamin B3 also called, and what does it help form?
cards.back: Niacin; it contributes to NAD and NADP, coenzymes used in metabolic reactions.

cards.front: Which deficiency causes pellagra?
cards.back: Severe niacin deficiency; the classic pattern includes dermatitis, diarrhea, and neurologic changes.

cards.front: What is vitamin B5 also called?
cards.back: Pantothenic acid, a component of coenzyme A.

cards.front: What are key functions of vitamin B6?
cards.back: Amino acid metabolism, neurotransmitter synthesis, and heme synthesis.

cards.front: What is vitamin B7 commonly called?
cards.back: Biotin, a cofactor for several carboxylase enzymes.

cards.front: What is vitamin B9 commonly called?
cards.back: Folate; folic acid is a form used in many supplements and fortified foods.

cards.front: Why is folate important for rapidly dividing cells?
cards.back: It supports one-carbon transfer reactions needed for DNA synthesis and normal cell division.

cards.front: Why is adequate folate especially important around conception?
cards.back: It helps reduce the risk of neural tube defects during early fetal development.

cards.front: Which foods commonly provide folate?
cards.back: Legumes, leafy green vegetables, and fortified grain products.

cards.front: What are key functions of vitamin B12?
cards.back: Normal red blood cell formation, nervous-system function, and DNA synthesis through its metabolic roles.

cards.front: Which foods reliably provide vitamin B12?
cards.back: Animal-derived foods and foods specifically fortified with B12; unfortified plant foods are not reliable sources.

cards.front: What stomach protein is important for normal vitamin B12 absorption?
cards.back: Intrinsic factor, which supports B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.

cards.front: How do folate and vitamin B12 deficiencies overlap and differ?
cards.back: Both can cause megaloblastic anemia; B12 deficiency can also cause important neurologic injury.

cards.front: What are key functions of vitamin C?
cards.back: Collagen synthesis, antioxidant activity, and improved absorption of nonheme iron.

cards.front: Which deficiency causes scurvy?
cards.back: Vitamin C deficiency.

cards.front: Which foods commonly provide vitamin C?
cards.back: Citrus fruits, peppers, kiwifruit, strawberries, and broccoli.

cards.front: What is a major structural role of calcium?
cards.back: It is a major component of bones and teeth.

cards.front: What functions does calcium have outside the skeleton?
cards.back: It contributes to muscle contraction, nerve signaling, and blood clotting.

cards.front: Which foods can provide calcium?
cards.back: Dairy products, calcium-set tofu, some fortified beverages, and certain leafy greens.

cards.front: What are important roles of phosphorus?
cards.back: It contributes to bones, teeth, ATP, nucleic acids, and phospholipids.

cards.front: What are important roles of magnesium?
cards.back: It supports many enzyme reactions, energy metabolism, and normal nerve and muscle function.

cards.front: Which foods commonly provide magnesium?
cards.back: Nuts, seeds, legumes, whole grains, and leafy green vegetables.

cards.front: What is a major role of sodium?
cards.back: It helps maintain extracellular fluid balance and supports nerve and muscle function.

cards.front: What is a major role of potassium?
cards.back: It helps maintain intracellular fluid balance and supports electrical activity in nerves and muscles.

cards.front: Which foods commonly provide potassium?
cards.back: Potatoes, beans, lentils, many fruits, vegetables, and dairy foods.

cards.front: What is a role of chloride?
cards.back: It contributes to fluid and acid-base balance and is a component of stomach acid.

cards.front: Why is iron necessary for oxygen transport?
cards.back: Iron is part of heme in hemoglobin and myoglobin.

cards.front: How do heme and nonheme iron differ in food sources?
cards.back: Heme iron occurs in animal tissues; nonheme iron occurs in plant foods and also in some animal foods.

cards.front: What food component can improve nonheme iron absorption?
cards.back: Vitamin C consumed with the meal.

cards.front: What is a major consequence of iron deficiency?
cards.back: It can cause iron-deficiency anemia and associated fatigue and reduced functional capacity.

cards.front: Why is iodine needed?
cards.back: It is required to make thyroid hormones.

cards.front: What are common dietary iodine sources?
cards.back: Iodized salt, seafood, dairy products, and some other foods; amounts vary by food and region.

cards.front: What are important roles of zinc?
cards.back: It supports enzyme activity, immune function, wound healing, and normal growth.

cards.front: What is a major function of selenium?
cards.back: It is part of selenoproteins involved in antioxidant defenses and thyroid hormone metabolism.

cards.front: What are important roles of copper?
cards.back: It supports iron metabolism, connective tissue formation, and several enzyme systems.

cards.front: How does fluoride help teeth?
cards.back: Appropriate exposure supports enamel resistance to acid-related decay.

cards.front: What is an electrolyte?
cards.back: A substance that forms electrically charged ions in solution, such as sodium or potassium salts.

cards.front: Why is water essential even though it provides no calories?
cards.back: It supports transport, temperature regulation, chemical reactions, and fluid balance.

cards.front: What is energy balance?
cards.back: The relationship between energy intake and energy expenditure over time.

cards.front: What is nutrient density?
cards.back: The amount of beneficial nutrients a food provides relative to its energy content or another stated quantity.

cards.front: How does a serving size differ from a portion size?
cards.back: Serving size is a defined reference amount; portion size is the amount someone actually chooses to eat.

cards.front: Does a multivitamin replace a varied diet?
cards.back: No. Foods also provide fiber, energy, and many components that a multivitamin does not supply.

cards.front: What does an upper intake level mean?
cards.back: The highest average daily intake generally unlikely to pose harm for most people in a specified group; it is not an intake goal.
